title: Prehistoric Life · Episode 2
chapters: Ice Age giants and Australia's megafauna

units.t: Prehistoric Life. Episode two.
In this episode: The day the dinosaurs died and Ice Age giants and Australia's megafauna.
Part one. The day the dinosaurs died.
Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about 10 kilometres wide slammed into Mexico.
Within a short time, around three-quarters of species on Earth were gone.
The iridium clue.
Geologists long noticed a sharp line in the rock record at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago.
Below it are dinosaurs, ammonites and marine reptiles; above it, they are gone.
Around three-quarters of species vanished, including every non-bird dinosaur, the pterosaurs and sea reptiles like mosasaurs.
It is the most recent of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.
In 1980, Luis Alvarez, his son Walter, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel found unusually high iridium in the boundary clay near Gubbio, Italy.
It is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids.
The spike appeared in Denmark, New Zealand and elsewhere, pointing to an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide.
Many geologists remained sceptical.
Finding the crater.
The missing piece was a crater.
In the late 1970s, geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company had noticed a giant buried ring structure.
In 1991, researchers linked it to the extinction.
Named after the nearby town of Chicxulub, the crater is about 180 kilometres across, mostly hidden under younger rock and the Gulf of Mexico sea floor.
Dating shows it formed right at the boundary.
Evidence piled up: 'shocked' quartz grains that form only under extreme pressure, glassy spherules of melted rock, and jumbled tsunami deposits around the Gulf.
In 2016, an expedition drilled into the crater's peak ring.
What the impact did.
The asteroid released far more energy than all the world's nuclear weapons combined.
Nearby came huge tsunamis and earthquakes, and falling molten debris likely ignited widespread fires.
The biggest killer was probably what followed.
The target rocks were rich in sulfur, and the blast lofted sulfur aerosols, soot and dust into the atmosphere.
This blocked sunlight, cooled the planet for years and shut down much of photosynthesis.
When plants and plankton failed, food chains collapsed from the bottom up.
At the same time, eruptions in India built the Deccan Traps, releasing carbon dioxide and sulfur gases.
Their role is contested, though most researchers see the asteroid as the main trigger.
Survivors and successors.
Survival was not random.
On land, almost nothing larger than about 25 kilograms is thought to have made it.
Small animals needed less food, bred quickly and could shelter in burrows or water.
Crocodiles, turtles and frogs fared relatively well, likely because their food webs relied on dead plant matter.
Some ground-dwelling birds did better than tree-dwellers because forests were devastated.
In the oceans, ammonites vanished, while sharks and many fish survived.
Mammals, mostly small and nocturnal for over 100 million years, spread into empty roles.
Within about 15 million years they had produced early horses, primates and whale ancestors.
Our existence owes something to a very bad day.
Could it happen again.
Asteroids of Chicxulub's size are thought to hit Earth roughly once every 100 million years or so, so the risk in any lifetime is tiny.
Astronomers have found the great majority of near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre, and none are known to be on a collision course.
Smaller objects are more common: the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor in Russia injured over 1,000 people, mostly from shattered glass.
In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into a small asteroid called Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around a larger companion by about 32 minutes.
For the first time, a species has shown it can deflect an asteroid.
The key idea: About 66 million years ago a mass extinction ended the Cretaceous, and a worldwide iridium layer pointed to an asteroid.
Part two. Ice Age giants and Australia's megafauna.
Rhino-sized wombat relatives, a marsupial 'lion' and a goanna the length of a car once roamed Australia.
So where did they all go?
Giants of the Ice Age.
Megafauna simply means 'big animals', often defined as over about 45 kilograms.
The term usually refers to the giants of the Pleistocene, the epoch of repeated ice ages from about 2.
6 million to roughly 11,700 years ago.
In the last 50,000 years or so, a large share of them disappeared.
Unlike dinosaurs, they lived alongside humans, which makes their fate one of science's most debated questions.
Across Europe, Asia and North America lived woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and cave bears.
The giant deer Megaloceros had antlers spanning up to about 3.
5 metres.
Sabre-toothed cats such as Smilodon hunted in the Americas.
Early humans painted many of these animals at Chauvet and Lascaux in France.
Australia's marsupial giants.
Australia's megafauna were dominated by giant marsupials.
Diprotodon, a distant relative of wombats, was the largest marsupial ever, roughly rhinoceros-sized and up to about 2.
7 tonnes.
Dozens of skeletons came from the dry bed of Lake Callabonna in South Australia, where animals likely became trapped in mud.
Procoptodon goliah was a short-faced kangaroo about 2 metres tall.
Thylacoleo, the 'marsupial lion', was not a cat but a relative of wombats and koalas.
Weighing roughly 100 kilograms or more, it had blade-like cheek teeth, a hooked thumb claw and one of the most powerful bites for its body size.
Megalania, Varanus priscus, a giant goanna, may have reached 4 to 7 metres, though estimates vary.
Genyornis, the thunder bird.
Genyornis newtoni stood about 2 metres tall and weighed perhaps 200 kilograms or more, far heavier than an emu.
Despite appearances, it belonged to an extinct group called dromornithids, or mihirungs, whose closest living relatives are ducks and geese, not emus.
Its 'thunder bird' relatives had lived in Australia for millions of years.
Scientists argued over burnt eggshell fragments, around 50,000 years old, that seemed to show early people cooking Genyornis eggs.
A 2016 study proposed they came from a giant megapode instead, but a 2022 analysis of ancient proteins in the shells confirmed they belonged to Genyornis.
It shows how carefully evidence must be read.
Why did they vanish.
Most of Australia's megafauna seem to have gone by roughly 40,000 years ago, after people arrived at least 50,000 years ago.
One view blames hunting, even at low levels, tipping slow-breeding giants into decline, plus burning that changed habitats.
Another points to a drier, more variable climate.
Many researchers now favour a combination, varying by species and place.
Dating fossils this old is hard, which keeps the debate alive.
Island cases are clearer.
New Zealand's moa, some standing over 2 metres tall, became extinct within roughly 200 years of Polynesian settlement around 1300 AD.
Madagascar lost its giant elephant birds after people arrived.
Africa, where humans evolved, kept more of its megafauna.
Seeing them today.
You can see Australia's megafauna up close.
The Naracoorte Caves in South Australia and the Riversleigh fossil fields in north-west Queensland were jointly World Heritage-listed in 1994 as the Australian Fossil Mammal Sites.
At Naracoorte, animals fell through openings into the caves over hundreds of thousands of years, preserving an extraordinary record of the animals that lived nearby.
Museums across Australia display Diprotodon skeletons and casts.
There is a lesson for today too.
Large, slow-breeding animals are especially vulnerable to rapid change, whether from hunting, habitat loss or a shifting climate.
The key idea: Megafauna are large animals, usually over about 45 kilograms, and the Ice Age Northern Hemisphere had woolly mammoths, giant deer and sabre-toothed cats.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why was iridium in the boundary layer such an important clue?
Answer. Rare in Earth's crust, common in asteroids.
Question two. Why is the fate of Ice Age megafauna so debated, unlike that of the dinosaurs?
Answer. They lived alongside humans.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
